clean_story:
Warm dry gusts. Mountain weather shapers.

The name foehn comes from the Latin favonius, meaning a mild west wind, as these winds bring sudden warmth to valleys below. A foehn wind forms when moist air climbs a mountain, cools, and drops its water as rain or snow on the windward side. The now-dry air descends the leeward slope, warming rapidly—like a hairdryer blowing downhill. In the Alps, foehn winds can raise temperatures by 20 Celsius in an hour, melting snow and triggering avalanches. In California, the Santa Ana winds, a type of foehn, fan wildfires with their hot, dry blast. These winds also clear fog, sharpening visibility for pilots in places like New Zealand’s Southern Alps. Three related subjects are mountain waves, chinook winds and atmospheric rivers.
